strengths: Principled problem formulation: Framing concept shift diagnosis as learning a sparse additive correction to a fixed source-domain offset avoids the noise accumulation and sample inefficiency inherent to two-stage plugin approaches that fit separate source and target models.

Comprehensive methodological design: The paper provides a well-rounded suite of techniques, including standard L1 regularized estimation (SGShift), misspecification absorption (SGShift-A) to decouple source model misfit from genuine conditional shifts, and Model-X knockoffs (SGShift-K) for rigorous error control.

Solid theoretical grounding: The authors provide finite-sample estimation error bounds under restricted strong convexity (Theorems 3.1 and 3.2) as well as error-control guarantees (PFER and FDR via e-BH) for knockoff selection (Theorem 3.3).

Extensive empirical benchmarking: The evaluation tests 48 configurations (spanning combinations of linear models, trees, GBDTs, and SVMs), sparse vs. dense shifts, low-sample target regimes, high-dimensional settings, varying correlation, and varying SNR, consistently showing superior shifted-feature identification over baselines.

Convincing real-world applications: The case studies on COVID-19 hospitalization (pre/post-Omicron) and Lupus genetic risk across ancestries demonstrate that SGShift identifies clinically and biologically meaningful features, while showing on ACS Income that sparse updates recover >90% of target-domain performance loss.
weaknesses: Practical knockoff construction challenges: Model-X knockoffs theoretically require exact knowledge of the marginal target feature distribution P_T(X). In tabular data with mixed data types and complex dependencies, approximate knockoff samplers (e.g., second-order Gaussian or deep generative models) can lead to inflated false discovery rates; a discussion or empirical sensitivity analysis regarding knockoff approximation quality would strengthen the paper.

Expressiveness of the basis expansion: The generalized additive formulation relies on a specified basis map phi(X). While the authors show robustness to interaction terms in the appendix, severe non-additive or high-order interactive concept shifts may remain challenging to capture without rich basis engineering.

Baseline scope: While Diff, WhyShift, and SHAP-based attribution provide informative baselines, additional recent conditional shift attribution methods (e.g., loss-decomposition approaches like Singh et al., 2024) mentioned in related work are not included in the empirical benchmark tables.

Identifiability between source misfit and concept shift in SGShift-A: Decoupling shared misspecification from genuine target shift via the heuristic weighting parameter c = lambda_omega / lambda_delta relies on strong heuristic assumptions, which could be sensitive when the source model has substantial domain-specific underfitting.

strengths: Principled and elegant formulation: Framing concept shift diagnosis as learning a sparse additive correction offset by the source model neatly avoids error accumulation from independently fitting separate source and target models (a notable drawback of existing plugin methods like WhyShift).

Comprehensive framework: The manuscript thoughtfully addresses practical hurdles by introducing SGShift-A to absorb source model misspecification and SGShift-K to provide statistical false discovery rate control via Model-X knockoffs.

Solid theoretical support: The authors establish finite-sample high-dimensional M-estimation consistency rates for the correction vectors under cone-restricted strong convexity (Theorems 3.1 and 3.2) as well as error-control guarantees via knockoffs and e-BH aggregation (Theorem 3.3).

Extensive empirical benchmarking: The evaluation is exceptionally thorough, testing 48 model-generator combinations across multiple datasets, examining matched vs. mismatched architectures, sample size scaling, high dimensionality, collinearity, dense shifts, and varying SNR.

Insightful real-world validation: The empirical analysis demonstrates that real performance drops across 87 ACS Income shift benchmarks can be recovered with sparse updates, and the case studies (COVID-19 Omicron variant shift and Lupus ancestry-specific genetics) align well with established medical and biological literature.
weaknesses: Dependence on target labels: The method fundamentally requires labeled target data. While estimating conditional distribution shift P(Y|X) nonparametrically without labels is generally impossible, the required sample size and latency of acquiring target labels in practical streaming or deployment settings warrants a deeper discussion.

Expressiveness of the linear/additive correction: The shift model relies on a linear combination of basis functions phi(X). While the authors show empirical resilience to interaction terms in Appendix K, capturing complex, non-linear, and high-order interaction shifts in high-dimensional tabular data without combinatorial basis explosion remains a potential limitation.

Practical knockoff generation for tabular data: SGShift-K assumes exact Model-X knockoff generation. Constructing valid knockoffs for mixed continuous and categorical tabular data with intricate dependencies is non-trivial, and approximation errors in the knockoff generator can lead to inflated false discovery rates in practice.

Minor presentation issues: In Section 3.4 / 4 (page 5), the text under Theorem 3.3 states 'Theorem 3.2 guarantees per family error rate...', which is a slight numbering typo referring to Theorem 3.3. In addition, sub-panels in Figure 3 are quite compact and difficult to read without zooming.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Diagnosing and attributing concept shift (changes in conditional distribution P(Y|X)) to specific interpretable features is a critical challenge in ML reliability, medical informatics, and scientific discovery, where marginal covariate shift methods fall short.

Sound and elegant formulation: Instead of relying on error-prone plug-in differences of two separately estimated models (such as WhyShift or difference-of-SHAPs), SGShift frames the problem as learning a sparse residual update on the link scale, allowing the reuse of mature high-dimensional estimation and variable selection techniques.

Principled variants: The paper introduces SGShift-A to absorb shared source model misspecification and SGShift-K using Model-X knockoffs with e-BH aggregation to provide rigorous false discovery rate (FDR) control.

Thorough experimental benchmarking: The evaluation includes semi-synthetic simulations under 16 model combinations across multiple healthcare datasets, stress-testing under dense shifts, low target sample sizes, high feature correlations, and varying signal-to-noise ratios, along with qualitative case studies in COVID-19 and Lupus genomics.
weaknesses: Knockoff generation and distribution estimation: SGShift-K assumes the ability to generate valid Model-X knockoffs, which requires accurate modeling of the target feature distribution P_T(X). In complex tabular domains with mixed data types and non-Gaussian dependencies, knockoff construction errors can lead to inflated FDR or loss of power; this practical challenge is insufficiently analyzed.

Linear/GAM link-scale parameterization: The method models the shift contrast as linear in the basis phi(X). If the true concept shift is highly non-linear or involves complex high-order feature interactions outside the pre-specified basis, the sparse attribution may select surrogate/correlated features or fail to capture the shift mechanism.

Baseline scope: While comparisons against Diff, WhyShift, and SHAP are informative, the experimental comparison lacks other recent attribution and shift-decomposition methods mentioned in the related work (e.g., Singh et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023) or standard penalized transfer learning baselines.

Theoretical assumptions for stability selection: In Theorem 3.3, assuming that per-repeat false-selection events are independent across knockoff repeats with bounded uniform probability is an idealized assumption in the stability selection heuristic, rather than an unconditional finite-sample property stemming purely from knockoff exchangeability.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Diagnosing and attributing concept shift ($P(y|X)$ shift) to a sparse set of features is crucial for debugging machine learning models in practice and for scientific discovery, yet most prior literature focuses predominantly on covariate shift ($P(X)$) or detection without attribution.

Principled methodology: The proposed SGShift formulation elegantly poses the problem as learning a sparse additive correction over an existing source model $\hat{f}$, and the extensions—SGShift-A (absorption term for source model misspecification) and SGShift-K/KA (knockoffs with stability selection for false discovery control)—are well-conceived and address key practical challenges.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The semi-synthetic benchmark covers 16 combinations of generator and base models across three distinct real-world healthcare datasets (spanning classification and regression). The empirical gains in AUC and recall over baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP) are consistent and substantial.

Validation of real-world sparsity and interpretability: The analysis in Figure 2 demonstrates that selective feature updates capture the bulk of performance recovery under natural shift, and the qualitative case study on COVID-19 severity (Omicron vs. Delta) aligns well with established clinical literature.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in GAM basis representation and feature grouping: Section 3.2 defines the shift via $K$ basis functions $\phi(X_i)$, but the text does not detail what basis functions are used in the experiments (e.g., linear basis, splines, or kernel expansions). If multi-dimensional basis expansions per feature are used ($K > p$), standard $\ell_1$ penalty selects individual basis coefficients rather than entire features, which would require group-lasso regularization. The exact parametrization and mapping from basis coefficients to feature selection should be made explicit.

Theoretical gap in Lemma 4.2 (FDR bound): In Appendix A.4, the proof for FDR control factors the expectation as $\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{V^{[b]}}{R^{[b]}\vee 1}\cdot R^{[b]}\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[R^{[b]}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{V^{[b]}}{R^{[b]}\vee 1}\mid R^{[b]}\right]\right] \le \mathbb{E}[R^{[b]}\cdot q]$. Standard knockoff theory (e.g., Candès et al., 2018) establishes marginal control $\mathbb{E}[V/(R\vee 1)] \le q$, not conditional control given the rejection count $R$. Since $V/(R\vee 1)$ and $R$ are generally dependent, this inequality does not immediately follow without additional regularity conditions or bounding techniques (as discussed in the derandomized knockoffs literature).

Evaluation alignment with model assumptions: In the semi-synthetic simulations, target shifts are generated by perturbing $g(\mathbb{E}[y|X])$ additively through selected features. Because the data generating process adheres closely to the additive linear-in-parameter assumption of SGShift, it inherently favors the proposed method over non-parametric or heuristic baselines like WhyShift and SHAP.

Missing details on knockoff generation for tabular data: Generating valid Model-X knockoffs for heterogeneous tabular datasets (containing mixed continuous, discrete, and correlated binary features) is non-trivial. The paper does not specify which knockoff generator was employed (e.g., second-order Gaussian knockoffs, copula knockoffs, or deep generative models) or assess sensitivity to knockoff approximation errors.

strengths: Important and timely problem formulation: diagnosing and attributing concept shift ($P(y|X)$ shift) to a sparse set of interpretable features in tabular data, moving beyond detection or pure covariate shift adaptation.
The conceptual framework is modular and thoughtful, combining an additive shift term with an absorption mechanism (SGShift-A) to decouple base model misspecification from genuine distribution shift.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple real-world healthcare datasets (Diabetes Readmission, COVID-19 Hospitalization, SUPPORT2) tested across 16 combinations of generator and base model architectures.
Clear writing, logical progression of ideas, and well-motivated case studies connecting selected features to domain literature (e.g., COVID-19 severity shifts during the Omicron wave).
weaknesses: Fundamental mathematical errors in the proof of Lemma 4.2 (Appendix A.4): The proof for FDR control under stability selection contains critical flaws. First, it claims that $|\hat{A}(\pi)| \vee 1 \ge B\pi$ to bound the denominator, which is incorrect because $|\hat{A}(\pi)|$ is the number of selected features, while $B\pi$ is the threshold on per-feature selection frequency across $B$ knockoff runs. Second, the proof uses a lower bound on $\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbb{E}[R^{[b]}]$ from the geometric thinning inequality to establish an upper bound on FDR, which reverses the inequality. Finally, terms including $\mathbb{E}[|\hat{A}(\pi)|]$ and $\pi$ are dropped arbitrarily to force the expression $\frac{q}{1-(1-\pi)^B}$. Consequently, the claim of rigorous FDR control is unproven.

Ambiguity regarding the GAM basis functions $\phi(X)$: The paper introduces the method under the Generalized Additive Model (GAM) framework with basis functions $\phi(X) \in \mathbb{R}^K$. However, the manuscript never specifies what basis functions are used in practice (e.g., splines, polynomials, or raw features). If splines are used, an entrywise $\ell_1$ penalty does not yield feature-level sparsity (a group lasso penalty over basis expansions per feature would be required). If $\phi(X) = X$, the model is simply a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) rather than a GAM.

Lack of essential simulation details: Section 5 states that target labels are generated by 'perturbing $g(\mathbb{E}[y|X])$ through additive transformations based on selected input features.' However, the text omits how many features were shifted, how they were chosen, and what specific transformation functions and magnitudes were applied. Furthermore, simulating shifts through additive perturbations directly matches the structural assumptions of SGShift, giving it an inherent advantage over general baselines.

Missing details on knockoff generation for tabular data: Generating Model-X knockoffs for tabular datasets containing mixed discrete, categorical, and continuous variables is non-trivial and requires careful estimation of $P(X)$. The paper does not describe how knockoffs were generated in the experiments or whether exchangeability was validated.

Overstated conclusions regarding real-world sparsity: The interpretation of Figure 2 as 'verifying the sparsity of true concept shift' is unsupported. Observing diminishing returns (an elbow curve) when adding features to minimize validation loss is standard behavior in regularized regression due to bias-variance tradeoff and does not constitute proof that the underlying concept shift is intrinsically sparse.

strengths: Important problem formulation: Attributing concept shift (changes in the conditional distribution P(y|X)) to specific features is an essential, practical problem in ML safety and domain adaptation, where prior work has largely focused on covariate shift or detection rather than interpretable attribution.

Modular framework: The proposed SGShift formulation naturally decomposes the shift into an interpretable additive update over an existing source model, with well-motivated extensions: an absorption term to mitigate source model misspecification and knockoffs to provide error control.

Extensive empirical comparisons across model types: The experimental evaluation tests multiple distinct base and generator model architectures (trees, SVMs, linear models, gradient boosting) across three real-world healthcare datasets.
weaknesses: Severe theoretical errors in Lemma 4.2 (FDR Control for Derandomized Knockoffs): The proof on page 14 contains fatal mathematical flaws. First, it asserts that E[V^[b] / (R^[b] \vee 1) | R^[b]] <= q to pull q out of the expectation, but knockoff theory only guarantees marginal FDR control, not conditional FDR given the number of rejections R^[b]. Second, the authors cite the geometric thinning lower bound on \sum E[R^[b]] from Ren et al. (2023) and substitute it into an upper bound, which reverses the inequality. Derandomizing knockoffs while maintaining finite-sample FDR control is a known open/difficult challenge in statistics (which is why Ren et al., 2023 focus on PFER and e-values), and the claimed bound is mathematically invalid.

Inconsistencies and unverified assumptions in Theorem 4.1: The subgradient bound ||\nabla L(\delta^*)||_\infty <= c_3 \lambda is stated as an assumption rather than proven from design and noise concentration. Furthermore, the loss L is defined as an unnormalized sum \sum_{i=1}^{n_T} \ell_i, producing a denominator of c_1 n_T - 4 c_2 a, yet \lambda is specified with the rate \sqrt{\log K / n_T} (standard for normalized 1/n_T losses). Without normalizing the empirical loss, the gradient norm scales as \sqrt{n_T \log K}, making the stated rates and constants inconsistent.

Synthetic data generation strongly favors SGShift by construction: In the semi-synthetic experiments, target distributions are generated by perturbing g(E[y|X]) via additive transformations of selected input features. This directly matches the parametric assumption of SGShift (g(E_T[y|X]) = f(X) + \phi(X)^T \delta), whereas competing baselines (WhyShift, SHAP difference) are non-parametric or heuristic. This setup virtually guarantees that the proposed method will dramatically outperform baselines.

Ambiguity in basis function implementation and GAM definition: The paper describes the framework as a Generalized Additive Model (GAM), but does not specify the basis functions \phi(X) used in the experiments. If \phi(X) consists of univariate non-linear splines (K > p), coordinate-wise knockoffs and standard lasso selection do not control feature-level false discovery (group knockoffs are required). If \phi(X) is simply the original linear features (K = p), the model is a penalized GLM rather than a GAM.

Flawed claim regarding sparsity in real data: In Section 6, the authors assert that Figure 2 demonstrates that concept shift in real data is sparse because model performance displays an 'elbow shape' as the regularization penalty loosens. An elbow curve is a standard symptom of the bias-variance tradeoff / overfitting when fitting additional parameters on finite target samples; it does not constitute valid proof of underlying sparsity in the data generating process.
